name: Windows Deployment and Disk Management
summary: Windows Server is installed from an image, configured with roles and features, and stores data on basic or dynamic disks with MBR or GPT partitioning.

sections.title: Editions and installation
points: Main Windows Server editions: Standard and Datacenter; Datacenter adds unlimited virtual machine rights.
Two install options: Desktop Experience (full GUI) and Server Core (command line, less attack surface).
Minimum practical requirements: 64-bit CPU, 2 GB+ RAM, 32 GB+ disk and a network adapter.
Modern servers boot with UEFI + GPT; older BIOS systems use MBR.
Unattended installation uses an answer file (autounattend.xml); image files are install.wim or install.esd.
After installation, activate Windows with a retail key, MAK (multiple activation key) or KMS (key management service).

sections.title: Roles and features
points: Server Manager installs roles (big services such as AD DS, DNS, DHCP) and features (smaller add-ons).
PowerShell equivalent: Install-WindowsFeature (older) or Install-WindowsFeature / Add-WindowsFeature via Server Manager module.
A role can add dependent features automatically (for example DNS adds the DNS Server tools).
Roles are removed with Remove-WindowsFeature; data and configuration are not always removed with them.
Server Core is managed remotely with Server Manager, RSAT, PowerShell remoting or sconfig.

sections.title: Disks and partitions
points: Basic disk uses primary partitions (maximum 4) and an extended partition with logical drives.
MBR supports 4 primary partitions and disks up to 2 TB.
GPT supports up to 128 partitions and disks larger than 2 TB, and stores backup partition data.
System partition holds boot files; boot partition holds the Windows folder (names are the reverse of what people expect).
A dynamic disk supports simple, spanned, striped (RAID 0), mirrored (RAID 1) and RAID 5 volumes.
Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) and diskpart manage disks, partitions and drive letters.

sections.title: Filesystems and quotas
points: NTFS supports permissions, encryption (EFS), compression, quotas and journaling.
FAT32 is limited to 4 GB per file and is used for small removable drives.
exFAT removes the 4 GB limit and is good for large removable media, but has no NTFS permissions.
Disk quotas are configured per volume, not per folder, and can warn a user before denying writes.
Shadow copies keep previous versions of files for quick restore.
Cluster size is the smallest disk unit allocated to a file; a large cluster wastes space on small files.

name: Windows DNS
summary: DNS turns names into IP addresses. Windows DNS Server hosts forward and reverse zones, caches answers and integrates with Active Directory and DHCP.

sections.title: Zones
points: Forward lookup zone: name to IP. Reverse lookup zone: IP to name, stored under in-addr.arpa.
Primary zone is a writable copy of the zone; secondary zone is a read-only copy updated by zone transfer.
AD-integrated zone stores records in Active Directory and replicates with AD instead of zone transfers.
Stub zone keeps only the name-server records needed to find the authoritative server.
Conditional forwarder forwards queries for one domain to a specific DNS server.
A zone starts with an SOA record and NS records that describe the zone and its name servers.

sections.title: Records and queries
points: A record maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA maps to an IPv6 address.
CNAME is an alias pointing to another name; MX points to a mail server.
PTR is used for reverse lookup; SRV records tell clients where services (LDAP, Kerberos) are.
SOA contains the serial number and timers: refresh, retry, expire and minimum TTL.
Recursive query: the server finds the full answer for the client. Iterative query: the server returns the next server to ask.
The DNS cache stores answers until the TTL expires; ipconfig /flushdns clears it.
ipconfig /registerdns makes a client register its own A and PTR records.

sections.title: Zone transfer and maintenance
points: The secondary server checks the primary by comparing the SOA serial number.
Refresh interval sets how often the secondary checks the primary for changes.
Retry interval is how long it waits after a failed check; expire time stops answering if the master is unreachable.
AXFR transfers the whole zone; IXFR transfers only changes.
Forwarders and root hints resolve names the server does not host.
Scavenging removes stale dynamic records; DHCP can update DNS records for clients (dynamic update).
nslookup and Resolve-DnsName test name resolution.

name: Windows DHCP
summary: DHCP gives clients an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers automatically using the DORA process.

sections.title: Lease process
points: DORA: Discover (client broadcast) -> Offer (server) -> Request (client) -> Acknowledge (server).
DHCPv4 uses UDP port 67 on the server and 68 on the client; DHCPv6 uses 547 and 546.
At 50% of the lease the client renews; at 87.5% it rebinds with any server.

sections.title: Scopes and options
points: A scope is the range of addresses a server hands out for one subnet.
Exclusions remove addresses from the range; reservations always give one address to a fixed MAC.
Common options: 003 router (default gateway), 006 DNS servers, 015 DNS domain name, 051 lease time.
Default lease time is 8 days on Windows Server.
A superscope groups several scopes on one physical network.
Multicast scope hands out multicast addresses instead of unicast addresses.

sections.title: Server-side concepts
points: A DHCP server must be authorised in Active Directory before it can give addresses.
A relay agent (or IP helper on a router) forwards DHCP messages between subnets.
A DHCP failover partnership shares scopes between two servers (load balance or hot standby).
Split scope divides the range between two servers for extra resilience.
DHCP can register client records in DNS on behalf of the client (always, or only if the client asks).
ipconfig /release gives up the lease; ipconfig /renew asks for a new one.

name: Active Directory Domain Services
summary: AD DS is a directory service that stores users, computers and policies in a hierarchical database and controls domain logon with Kerberos and LDAP.

sections.title: Logical and physical structure
points: Forest is the top-level container; a tree is a set of domains sharing a namespace; a domain is the main administrative boundary.
Organizational units (OUs) group objects for delegation and Group Policy.
A site represents a physical network with good connectivity; site links connect sites for replication.
The schema defines which attributes an object can have.
The global catalog is a partial copy of every object in the forest used for fast searches.
Each domain has at least one domain controller (DC) holding a writable copy of the directory.

sections.title: Replication and FSMO roles
points: Intra-site replication happens quickly (about every 15 seconds) and compresses only between sites.
Inter-site replication is scheduled and compressed to save bandwidth; the KCC builds the topology.
Five FSMO roles: Schema Master and Domain Naming Master (one per forest), RID Master, PDC Emulator and Infrastructure Master (one per domain).
The PDC Emulator is the time source for the domain and handles urgent password changes.
The RID Master hands out blocks of relative IDs for new security principals.
repadmin /showrepl and dcdiag check replication and DC health.

sections.title: Accounts, groups and trusts
points: Group scopes: global (forest-wide membership view), domain local (used on resources) and universal (forest-wide).
AGDLP rule: Accounts go into Global groups, Global groups go into Domain Local groups, Permissions are given to Domain Local groups.
A trust lets users in one domain authenticate in another; a forest trust links two forests.
Kerberos (port 88) is the default authentication protocol; LDAP (389/636) is used for directory queries.
DNS must work for AD: DCs register SRV records under _msdcs.
Deleted objects go to the Recycle Bin (if enabled) and can be restored with ADAC or Restore-ADObject.

sections.title: Administration tools
points: dsa.msc = Active Directory Users and Computers; dssite.msc = Sites and Services; domains.msc = Domains and Trusts.
ADAC (Active Directory Administrative Center) is the modern management console.
ntdsutil performs database maintenance, authoritativere restore and FSMO seizure.
PowerShell helpers: Get-ADUser, New-ADUser, Add-ADGroupMember, Get-ADDomainController.
Group Policy (gpmc.msc) is used to push settings to users and computers.

name: AD CS, ADFS, SCCM, Containers and NLB
summary: Beyond AD DS, Windows Server provides certificate services, federated identity, system management, container hosting and network load balancing.

sections.title: Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)
points: A certification authority (CA) issues and manages digital certificates.
Root CA signs its own certificate; a subordinate CA is signed by another CA.
Enterprise CA integrates with AD (auto-enrollment); standalone CA does not need AD.
Certificate templates define how certificates are requested and used.
Auto-enrollment lets users and computers get certificates automatically through Group Policy.
CRL and OCSP let clients check whether a certificate has been revoked.

sections.title: Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS)
points: ADFS gives claims-based single sign-on between organizations and cloud applications.
A federation trust is created between a claims provider and a relying party.
Claims are statements about a user (name, email, group) issued after authentication.
ADFS supports SAML 2.0, WS-Federation and OAuth/OpenID Connect scenarios.
The ADFS proxy publishes federation services safely to the Internet.

sections.title: SCCM (Configuration Manager)
points: SCCM manages large Windows environments: inventory, software deployment, patching and OS deployment.
A central administration site (CAS) and primary sites organize the hierarchy.
Site systems include the management point (MP), distribution point (DP) and software update point (SUP).
Collections are groups of devices or users that receive deployments.
Task sequences automate operating-system deployment.
Clients find their site using boundary groups and network locations.

sections.title: Windows containers and NLB
points: Windows containers run isolated applications using OS-level isolation; no full OS per app.
Process isolation shares the host kernel; Hyper-V isolation uses a lightweight VM for stronger separation.
Images are built from a base image and stored in a registry; Docker Engine (or containerd) runs them.
Network Load Balancing (NLB) spreads traffic across several servers using a virtual cluster IP.
NLB hosts send heartbeats; a host is removed from the cluster if heartbeats stop.
Port rules and affinity (single, network or none) control how client traffic is distributed.

name: VPN, DFS and NPS/RADIUS
summary: Remote access with VPN, file sharing with DFS, and central authentication with Network Policy Server (RADIUS) are common Windows Server services.

sections.title: VPN
points: VPN creates an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network between a client and a server (remote access) or two sites (site-to-site).
PPTP is old and weak; L2TP/IPsec, SSTP, IKEv2 and Always On VPN are modern choices.
L2TP/IPsec uses UDP 500 and 4500 plus protocol 50 (ESP); SSTP uses TCP 443.
Authentication methods include MS-CHAPv2, EAP with certificates and PEAP.
RRAS (Routing and Remote Access Service) provides the VPN server role.
VPN clients can be pushed DNS servers and routes by the VPN server.

sections.title: DFS
points: DFS Namespaces (DFS-N) present shared folders from many servers as one logical namespace.
A namespace has a root and folders that point to folder targets on different servers.
DFS Replication (DFS-R) keeps folders in sync between servers using replication groups.
Replication can be full mesh or hub-and-spoke, and schedule/bandwidth limits protect WAN links.
Client referrals pick the nearest server (site awareness) for faster access.
DFS-N and DFS-R are often combined: single namespace plus replicated data.

sections.title: NPS and RADIUS
points: NPS (Network Policy Server) is Microsoft's RADIUS server for authentication, authorization and accounting.
RADIUS client devices (VPN server, wireless controller) must be registered in NPS with a shared secret.
Connection request policies decide which requests are handled by which NPS server.
Network policies contain conditions, constraints and settings (for example time limits or VLAN assignment).
RADIUS uses UDP 1812 (authentication) and 1813 (accounting); the older ports are 1645/1646.
Certificate-based methods (PEAP-EAP-TLS) give the strongest wireless and VPN authentication.

name: PowerShell
summary: PowerShell is the Windows command-line shell and scripting language. Everything is an object, so output can be filtered, sorted and piped between commands.

sections.title: Cmdlets and help
points: Cmdlets use Verb-Noun naming, for example Get-Service, Set-Service, New-Item.
Get-Help shows help and examples; Get-Command finds commands; Get-Member lists object properties and methods.
Use -? for quick help, for example Get-Service -?.
PowerShell 7 is cross-platform (pwsh); Windows PowerShell 5.1 is built into Windows.
The execution policy controls whether scripts can run (Restricted, RemoteSigned, AllSigned, Unrestricted).

sections.title: Pipeline and objects
points: The pipeline | passes objects, not text, to the next command.
Where-Object filters objects; Select-Object picks properties; Sort-Object sorts; ForEach-Object processes each item.
Format-Table and Format-List only change display, not data.
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' | Select-Object Name is a typical one-liner.
Out-File and Export-Csv save output; Import-Csv reads data back.
Measure-Object counts and averages values.

sections.title: Variables, operators and flow
points: Variables start with $, for example $name = 'server01'.
Comparison operators: -eq, -ne, -gt, -lt, -like, -match, -contains.
Control flow: if/elseif/else, switch, foreach, while and do-while.
try/catch/finally handles errors; $Error stores recent errors.
Functions are defined with function Verb-Noun { param(...) ... }.
Modules group related commands; Install-Module adds new modules from the gallery.

sections.title: Remote administration
points: WinRM enables PowerShell remoting over TCP 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS).
Enable-PSRemoting configures the listener; Enter-PSSession opens an interactive remote session.
Invoke-Command runs a command or script block on one or many computers.
The Active Directory module provides cmdlets such as Get-ADUser and New-ADUser.
Scheduled tasks can run PowerShell with Register-ScheduledTask.
DSC (Desired State Configuration) declares the required state of servers and enforces it.

sections.title: Useful admin examples
points: Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' lists stopped services.
Get-EventLog -LogName System -Newest 20 (or Get-WinEvent) reads recent events.
New-LocalUser / Add-LocalGroupMember create and add local users.
Get-ChildItem -Recurse | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum reports folder size.
Restart-Computer -Force restarts a server; Stop-Computer shuts it down.
Invoke-Command -ComputerName SRV1 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service } runs a command remotely.
